extracted.intended_audience: judges and patent litigators drafting/using jury instructions
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent damages, including lost profits, reasonable royalty calculations, apportionment rules, and willful infringement guidance for use at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits—“But For” Test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lost profits, the plaintiff must show that, but for the defendant’s infringement, the plaintiff would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the sales of the allegedly infringing products made by the defendant. Plaintiff must prove this by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must determine what the parties who purchased/practiced the allegedly infringing product/method would have done if the infringement had not occurred. Emphasize that the profits referred to are those allegedly lost by the plaintiff, not profits made by the defendant on infringing sales. (Citations: Am. Seating; Aro; Ericsson; Tate.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits—Panduit Factors (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff has proven lost profits if it proves each of the Panduit factors by a preponderance of the evidence: demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market; absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes; plaintiff had the manufacturing and marketing ability to make all or part of the infringing sales; and the amount of profit plaintiff would have made but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will explain each factor in detail; plaintiff must prove each factor more likely than not. (Citations: Mentor Graphics; Rite-Hite; Panduit.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market, shown by significant sales of the plaintiff’s own patented product/method or significant sales of the defendant’s product/method covered by the asserted claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on defendant’s sales as proof, the plaintiff's and defendant's products/methods must be sufficiently similar to compete in the same market or segment. (Citations: DePuy Spine; BIC Leisure.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Acceptable Non-Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether non-infringing, acceptable substitutes competed with the defendant’s infringing product/method and what impact such substitutes would have had absent the defendant’s sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must have one or more advantages of the patented invention important to actual buyers, must not infringe (licensed or non-infringing), and must have been available during the damages period (need not have actually been sold). If not sold, defendant must show by preponderance that competitors had equipment/materials/know-how to make it during damages period. If some customers would likely have purchased substitutes, plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits for those sales. Even if plaintiff and defendant products were the only ones with patent advantages, plaintiff still must prove it would have made the defendant’s sales. (Citations: DePuy Spine; Grain Processing; Standard Havens; SmithKline.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Market Share (when substitutes exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: If acceptable non-infringing substitutes existed, plaintiff may be entitled to lost profits on a portion of infringing sales; plaintiff must prove it likely would have made a portion of the infringing sales equal to at least plaintiff’s share of the market but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must show it competed in the same market and could have captured that market share; it is not necessary to show only two suppliers in the market. (Citations: DePuy Spine; Ericsson; Crystal Semiconductor; BIC Leisure; State Indus.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must prove it had the manufacturing and marketing ability to supply the additional products/methods needed to make the sales it allegedly lost, or that someone working with plaintiff could have supplied them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must also prove it more likely than not had the ability to market and sell the additional products/methods. (Citations: Wechsler; Fonar; Datascope; Gyromat.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits—Amount of Profit—Incremental Income Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may calculate lost profits by determining lost sales and subtracting additional costs/expenses that would have been incurred to make those sales; lost profits cannot be speculative but need not be proven with unerring certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incremental income approach; consider costs that would have been incurred. (Citations: Kalman; King Instrument; Paper Converting; Bio-Rad; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Price Erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may recover additional damages if it proves that but for defendant’s infringement the plaintiff would have been able to charge higher prices or would not have had to lower its prices for its products/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award may equal difference between profits at the higher price and profits actually made at the lower price. If using higher price to determine lost sales/lost profits, must account for any decrease in plaintiff’s sales that might have occurred due to higher price. (Citations: Siemens; Ericsson; Vulcan; Rite-Hite; BIC Leisure; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff can recover additional damages for lost profits if it proves its costs (e.g., additional marketing costs) increased as a result of defendant’s infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that costs went up because of defendant’s actions and not for other reasons. (Citations: Amstar; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed Sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may seek damages for lost sales of collateral products ordinarily sold along with the patented product (collateral products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover lost profits for collateral products plaintiff must prove (1) it is more likely than not that it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral products and the product/method must be so closely related that they effectively act or are used together for a common purpose. Damages calculated same way as lost profits for the product/method. (Citations: DePuy Spine; Rite-Hite; State Indus.; Paper Converting.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the amount someone wanting to use the patented invention would have agreed to pay the patent owner and is the minimum amount of damages a patent owner can receive for an infringement; award must compensate for infringement and be at least a reasonable royalty for the use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royalty must be based on the incremental value the patented invention adds to the end product; when accused products have patented and unpatented features, the value added by patented features must be identified. Ultimate combination of royalty base and rate must reflect value attributable to infringing features and no more. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 284; Power Integrations; Exmark; Ericsson v. D-Link; VirnetX; Apple v. Motorola; Uniloc; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Using the 'Hypothetical Negotiation' Method
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between the plaintiff and the defendant, assuming they negotiated just before the infringement began, that the patent was valid and infringed, and both parties had full knowledge of the facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume parties willing to enter license and had full knowledge; this is a counterfactual construct to determine damages. (Citations: Apple v. Motorola; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Fujifilm; Lucent; Maxwell; Rite-Hite; Wang Labs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: royalties received by the licensor
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any royalties received by the licensor for licensing of the patent-in-suit, proving or tending to prove an established royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted license royalties can show an established royalty rate; must be supported by proper evidence. (Citations: LaserDynamics; Wordtech; ResQNet; Monsanto; Maxwell; TWM; Georgia-Pacific.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: defendant's rates on comparable patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the rates paid by the defendant to license other patents comparable to the patent-in-suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable licenses by defendant may inform reasonable royalty but differences must be accounted for. (Citations: Ericsson; Apple; LaserDynamics; ResQNet; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the nature and scope of the license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, restricted or unrestricted in territory or with respect to whom the manufactured product may be sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License terms (exclusivity, territory, field restrictions) affect royalty valuation and must be evaluated relative to the hypothetical license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: licensor’s policy and marketing program to preserve exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the licensor’s established policy and marketing program to maintain its right to exclude others from using the invention by not licensing others or by granting licenses under special conditions to preserve exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensor behavior regarding licensing (keep exclusive v. license broadly) affects expectations in negotiation and royalty valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: commercial relationship between licensor and licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the commercial relationship between the licensor and the licensee, such as whether they are competitors in the same territory and line of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive relationships can influence willingness to pay/accept royalties and licensing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: effect of patented product on collateral sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the effect of selling the patented product/method in promoting other sales of the licensee; the existing value of the invention to the licensor as a generator of sales of its non-patented items; and the extent of such collateral sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value from complementary/ancillary sales should be considered in royalty determination (collateral sales impact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: duration of the patent and term of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the duration of the patent and the term of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer remaining patent life or license term affects the present value of royalty stream and negotiation dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: established profitability/commercial success/popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the established profitability of the product made under the patent, its commercial success, and its popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success and profitability provide evidence of value of the patented invention to the marketplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: utility and advantages over prior modes/devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the utility and advantages of the patented invention over old modes or devices used for similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovative advantages and superior utility support higher valuation in negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: nature and character of commercial embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the nature of the patented invention; the character of the commercial embodiment of it as owned and produced by or for the licensor; and the benefits to those who have used the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How the invention is embodied/commercialized and user benefits are relevant to value attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: extent of defendant’s use of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent to which the defendant has made use of the invention and any evidence that shows the value of that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of actual use by defendant is probative of the economic value derived from the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: customary portion of profit/selling price for use of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of the profit or of the selling price that may be customary in the particular business or comparable businesses to allow for the use of the invention or analogous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry customs regarding acceptable profit shares for licensed technology can inform reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: portion of profit attributable to the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of the profit that arises from the patented invention itself as opposed to profit arising from unpatented features, manufacturing process, business risks, or improvements added by the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires apportionment: isolate profit specifically attributable to patented features versus other value drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: opinion testimony of qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the opinion testimony of qualified experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert economic testimony is admissible and relevant to reasonable royalty determinations; weight depends on reliability and factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: hypothetical agreed amount (prudent licensee/practically acceptable to patentee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the amount that a licensor and a licensee would have agreed upon at the time the infringement began if both sides had been reasonably and voluntarily trying to reach agreement—a royalty that a prudent licensee would pay and a patentee would accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core hypothetical-negotiation perspective: balance licensee’s ability to make profit and patentee’s willingness to license at acceptable terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific Factor: other economic factors a prudent business person would consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any other economic factor that a normally prudent business person would, under similar circumstances, take into consideration in negotiating the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended catchall for relevant economic evidence beyond enumerated factors. (Citations: LaserDynamics; Wordtech; ResQNet; Monsanto.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Attribution/Apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must be based on the value attributable to the patented technology, distinct from unpatented features or other factors such as marketing or defendant’s market position; royalty base and rate must reflect value attributable to the patented invention alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not choose an inappropriately high royalty base and reduce by low rate (or vice versa); royalty base must be closely tied to the invention and properly apportioned. (Citations: Power Integrations; Exmark; AstraZeneca; Ericsson v. D-Link; Apple v. Motorola; VirnetX; Versata; Uniloc; ResQNet; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally royalties should be based on the smallest salable unit that practices the patent and is closely related to the claimed invention; the entire market value rule is a narrow exception allowing damages based on entire product revenue only if the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates the value of the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the smallest salable unit is a multi-component product with non-infringing features, damages must be limited to value attributable to patented technology; EMVR applies only when patented feature solely drives demand. (Citations: Ericsson v. D-Link; VirnetX; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Lucent; Rite-Hite.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Multiple Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendant infringed multiple patents, the jury may award separate royalties for each infringed patent and consider evidence of number of licenses needed and effect on hypothetical negotiation of paying multiple royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider stacking/multiple-license dynamics in negotiation; evaluate need for multiple licenses and how that impacts rate. (Citations: Ericsson v. D-Link; Apple v. Motorola; Verizon v. Vonage; Stickle.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are not based on hindsight but on what the parties to the hypothetical negotiation would have agreed upon; evidence need not be limited to facts on or before the negotiation date—may include information parties reasonably would have foreseen, including post-negotiation usage, subsequent licenses, infringer profits, and non-infringing alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible to consider post-dating evidence that would have been foreseeable at negotiation time; avoid pure hindsight. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 284; Aqua Shield; Lucent; Studiengesellschaft; Sinclair.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Availability of Non-Infringing Substitutes (royalty context)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, consider evidence about availability and cost of acceptable non-infringing substitutes to the patented invention; an acceptable substitute must be licensed under the patent or not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability and cost of substitutes inform bargaining power and value attribution. (Citations: Prism Techs.; Mars; Zygo.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Use of Comparable License Agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider amounts that other parties paid for rights to the patents in question or similar technologies; a license need not be perfectly comparable to be considered, but differences must be accounted for when relying on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on prior licenses, adjust for differences in technologies, economic circumstances, and contracting parties before using them to set royalty. (Citations: Ericsson; Apple; LaserDynamics; ResQNet; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts Resolved Against Infringer (recordkeeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts about damages arising from the defendant’s failure to keep proper records should be resolved in favor of the plaintiff; confusion or difficulties caused by defendant’s records should be held against defendant, not plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adverse inference regarding damages when defendant’s poor recordkeeping prevents precise calculation. (Citations: Bigelow; Story Parchment; Minco; Sensonics; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) — Practice Note
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, jury instructions must address the particulars of any FRAND commitment made by the patentee, established principles of patent law, and only those Georgia‑Pacific factors relevant to the case; do not instruct on irrelevant Georgia‑Pacific factors. Jury must be instructed on apportionment both of the portion of the standard as a whole related to the patented technology and of the claimed invention versus value added by standardization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When SEPs are at issue, tailor instructions to FRAND commitments and apportionment of standard-related value; avoid irrelevant Georgia‑Pacific factors. (Citations: Commonwealth Sci. & Indus. Research Org. v. Cisco; Ericsson v. D-Link; Apple v. Motorola.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiff proves infringement of a valid claim by a preponderance, jury must determine whether infringement was willful. To show willfulness plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that defendant knew of plaintiff’s patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May consider malicious, wanton, deliberate, consciously wrongful, flagrant, or bad-faith behavior, but knowledge of the patent alone is insufficient. Assess all circumstances and defendant’s knowledge at the time of challenged conduct. If infringement found willful, it should not affect the amount of damages awarded by the jury. (Citations: Halo.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement—Reliance on Legal Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendant relies on a legal opinion to rebut willfulness, jurors may consider whether defendant reasonably relied on a competent legal opinion. If defendant does not rely on a legal opinion, absence of an opinion is not sufficient to find willfulness; the issue is whether all circumstances establish willful conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for 35 U.S.C. § 298 which bars using failure to obtain/present opinion of counsel as proof of willfulness; when opinion is offered, evaluate its reasonableness as one factor among the totality of circumstances. Modify instruction based on whether defendant asserts reliance on counsel. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 298; Halo.)
